But here’s the rub: what does "indie" even mean anymore? It’s as much a marketing term as it is a musical descriptor. You’ve got bands that are signed to major labels yet still carry that indie flag, like they’re in some kind of club where the rules are constantly rewritten. One fitting name for this eclectic mix could be "Indie Revival". This title captures the essence of what hipster music embodies: a revival of independent sounds that reject mainstream norms in favor of authenticity and originality. Answer_with_full_information: The term "hipster music" can be somewhat nebulous, as it encompasses a broad spectrum of sounds that appeal to those seeking something outside of mainstream trends. At its core, hipster music often celebrates authenticity, eclecticism, and a certain degree of irony. It can include genres like indie rock, lo-fi, and alternative folk, where artists often prioritize unique expression over commercial viability. But rather than a strict definition, it’s more about the attitude behind the music: an appreciation for the obscure, a penchant for vinyl records, and a love for the DIY ethic. Think of bands like Vampire Weekend or artists like Sufjan Stevens, whose sounds are layered with influences that might range from world music to classical, all while maintaining a certain quirkiness that feels refreshingly detached from the pop machine. This is music meant to be digested in a cozy coffee shop or at a small venue, where the connection between the artist and the audience is intimate rather than transactional. And let’s not forget the role of nostalgia; hipster music often draws on past musical eras, reinterpreting them with a modern twist. So, while there’s no singular name that can encapsulate this phenomenon, perhaps "alternative" or "indie" comes closest, as they reflect the musical diversity and cultural commentary that defines the hipster ethos. Ultimately, "hipster music" is less about a specific genre and more about a mindset that values originality, artistry, and a touch of counterculture rebellion.

Question: How would you rate the musicianship of jazz legend Charlie Parker? Does his legacy stand up even today with so many talented people playing now?
Old_Answer: You can tell the history of jazz in four words: Louis Armstrong, Charlie Parker. —Miles Davis Hi. Welcome to this answer. Please make yourself comfortable. We have some ground to cover. (Photo by William P. Gottlieb, source: [Portrait of Charlie Parker, Three Deuces, New York, N.Y., ca. Aug. 1947]) The Bare Minimum of Largely Unedifying Facts in the Case of Charles Parker Jr. Charlie Parker was born in Kansas City, Kansas, on August 29, 1920. His father Charles Sr was a dancer and singer and a serious alcoholic, and his mother Addie wouldn’t tolerate alcohol in the house. His parents separated, Charles Sr eventually becoming a chef on Pullman cars, which took him off around the country. Charles Jr began playing alto saxophone at the age of 11, but wasn’t very good at it. His mother bought him a new sax when he was 14, and he joined his high school band. In his mid-teens, he began to take music more seriously, and was taught the basics of improvisation by a local musician, trombonist Robert Simpson. Around this time, when he was first playing out as a musician, he got introduced to drugs. The same year, Parker proposed to his girlfriend, Rebecca Ruffin, and they were married. Again in 1936, on the way to a gig, he was in a car crash in which he broke three ribs. His effort to manage the pain may well have got him more dependent upon opioids. By 1937 he was addicted to heroin. At some point around this period, he adopted a regimen of practicing for several hours a day. He would sometimes vanish for days, because he was off practicing. His mother would go and find him and bring him home, he’d eat like a horse and then sleep for a couple of days, and then do it all over again. By 1937 he was working as a professional musician, actively seeking gigs. A residency in the Ozarks gave him ample practice time. In 1938 he joined Jay McShann’s band. In 1939 he went to New York City, where he worked for several months at several jobs, including dishwasher and washing cars. He was still practicing incessantly and playing at every opportunity he could find. His drug use slackened off, because he couldn’t afford them. All through his adult life, Parker alternated between being relatively clean, and using heroin. In 1940, he learned that his father had been stabbed to death. He returned to Kansas City for the funeral and rejoined Jay McShann’s band. While on tour with McShann he was introduced to Dizzy Gillespie, a trumpet player who was then with Cab Calloways’ orchestra. In 1942 Parker left McShann’s band and joined that of Earl Hines, a veteran pianist who’d played on many of Louis Armstrong’s classic early recordings. Here he played with Gillespie regularly for the first time: Gillespie had been fired from Calloway’s band after a misunderstanding that had led to a fight. In 1942, the American Federation of Musicians instituted a recording strike that would last until 1944. Parker left McShann’s band and started hanging out in New York with the group of musicians that centred around regular jam sessions in places like Minton’s Playhouse and Monroe’s Uptown House. (I wrote about this period in Alex Johnston's answer to What is Bebop in Jazz music?) The musicians at these sessions included Gillespie, pianist and composer Thelonious Monk, drummer Kenny Clarke, pianist Bud Powell, bassist Oscar Pettiford, and others. (Miles Davis joined the scene later on.) But these were not the only musicians who had been working towards taking jazz in a new direction, away from the riff-based swing that was then the dominant form of popular music in the Western world. Lots of other musicians had grown tired of swing and were pushing for something new. (This is amply documented in Gitler: see Sources.) It was into this situation that Parker arrived, having already made contact with Gillespie. He was almost immediately recognised by his peers as the dominant figure in the new music. From 1942 onwards, Parker, Gillespie and their colleagues made the first recordings of a new kind of jazz that would later be dubbed ‘bebop’, sometimes to the annoyance of the musicians themselves. Parker and Gillespie made many recordings together. In late 1946, Parker’s drug use became uncontrollable. He was asleep one night at the Civic Hotel when he accidentally set light to his mattress. He was arrested, beaten and jailed, then was checked into Camarillo State Hospital for six months. He got out in spring 1947, clean and healthy, and made dozens of recordings for the Savoy and Dial labels, with a band featuring Davis on trumpet and Max Roach on drums. For the next few years he continued to make the studio and live recordings which are the foundation of his legacy. He loved classical music, and made an album with a string section which was his most popular recording in his lifetime. He became tired of the limitations of three-minute recordings and song- and blues-based forms, and approached the modernist composer Edgard Varèse for music lessons. But he also went back to using drugs. When he wasn’t on drugs, he often drank to excess. At some point (I haven’t been able to find out when) he divorced his first wife Rebecca, married again (Doris) and divorced again, and then met his third and last partner Chan Richardson, with whom he had a daughter, Pree. Pree died in 1954 and Parker never got over her death. He attempted suicide twice and separated from Chan. In March 1955, he was at the apartment of his friend Nica de Koenigswarter, watching TV, when he had a heart attack and died. He was only 34 years old. The coroner who performed the autopsy had no idea of his birthdate, and estimated his age as being between 50 and 60. He is buried in Kansas City. For many years, his gravestone had the wrong date of death: March 23 instead of March 12. This was eventually fixed in 1992. However, the replacement gravestone bears an image of a tenor saxophone. Charlie Parker did not play the tenor sax. Not as his main instrument, anyway. His principal instrument was alto sax. Such were the fortunes of a jazz musician in the mid-20th century. Like so many lives of mid-20th century African-American jazz musicians, when you spell out the bare externals of Charlie Parker’s life like that, it’s mostly depressing. But what that story doesn’t tell you is what his impact was like on other people. What it was like to be around him. What people thought of him. You see, the opinions about Parker’s musicianship that truly matter, are not mine. What matters is the testimony of people who really knew his music, and understood from the inside what he was doing, and what made him different. Charlie Parker grew up in Kansas City. If we were to list only three cities in the USA which deserve to be regarded as true cradles of jazz, the first would be New Orleans, where jazz was created in the first place. The second would be New York City, where most great jazz musicians in the early/mid 20th century ended up coming to. The third would be Kansas City. In jazz terms, it was an astonishing combination of boot camp, battlefield and nursery. Stanley Crouch brilliantly describes Kansas City’s music scene in what I think is the best single book about Parker thus far for the general reader, Kansas City Lightning. Charlie Parker came out of Kansas City as one of those musicians who soaks up music more easily than other musicians do. When he was first living in New York in 1939, he attended a jam session at Dan Wall’s Chili House on Seventh Avenue and 140th Street, presided over by guitarist William ‘Biddy’ Fleet. Fleet noticed that Parker was interested in doing something unusual, and the thing that he really liked about Parker was that he didn’t need to go off and practice new ideas in privacy. He seemed to be able to absorb them instantly. His dexterity and the power of his playing became notorious. Many older sax players held their saxes at an angle in imitation of another of Parker’s influences, Lester Young, or otherwise posed while they played, or closed their eyes. Parker held his straight, and stared directly ahead while playing, and didn’t move, which earned him another nickname: Indian, after the wooden advertising figures used by tobacconists. During jam sessions among his friends, if things were getting competitive, someone would say ‘Go get Indian’, and Parker would be summoned from wherever he was practicing so that he could blow the interloper off the stage. His clean, aggressive tone makes his music stand out, especially on his many live recordings, where the rest of the band is sometimes a murky sound in the middle distance but he’s always there, in the foreground, his sax leaping up to the treble and then finding the most intricate and exploratory route down again. The jazz scholar Thomas Owens noted that Parker often accentuates the highest note in any phrase, and that’s one of the things that gives his playing that sense of soaring freedom, which in turn is why the nickname ‘Bird’ stuck to him. There are loads of stories about Parker’s negative personal habits: his tendency to pawn other people’s stuff so he could get money for drugs; his chronic lateness; his general unreliability as a human being; his greed (Miles Davis complains at length about this in his autobiography); his fatal susceptibility to his own appetites, which is maybe the same thing. There’s no getting around the fact that Parker as a human being was one of the legendary fuck-ups of jazz. The strange thing is that he’s not the kind of musician whose music was about how messed up he was. He’s not a Lester Young, or a Chet Baker, whose music seems to have functioned as a balm to their souls, a consolation for all the crap that they put up with. Parker’s tone is bright, aggressive and immensely confident. His music surges with life and power. It bucks you up. What was it like to be around that? The Testimonials It was one of the greatest uplifts of my life. Men like that just lift you up. It wouldn’t matter if they were playing with a washboard. They would still sound good. —Art Blakey, on the experience of playing with Charlie Parker It’s rare to get a genius on the scene. I guess not more than one will come along every quarter-century in any field you can think of. But Bird had all the necessary equipment. You could just follow the leader as far as Charlie Parker was concerned. —Kenny Clarke In my opinion, Bud (Powell) was a genius just like Bird. They were untouchable as far as their musicianship was concerned. They could do no wrong in anything they did, which was a hell of a mark for a young cat to try to achieve. —Sonny Rollins Bird used to come to Minton’s, and he was so great that everyone would leave the bandstand when he played. All the bad saxophone players showed him respect and let him have the bandstand. —Kenny Dorham The thing about Charlie Parker was that he was such a giant. He was so much better than everybody else. It’s not like there was this guy and that guy. There was everybody else, and there was Charlie. —Al Cohn [Parker] was always reading and learning. He was a very educated man. He could talk about—my car was goofing off and I said ‘Damn! I’m going to take this thing to the garage,’ and he said, ‘It ain’t nothin’ but such-and-such,’ and he got out there, and he went around the motor, and he fixed the damn thing! He knew all about the motor and what caused it to run and all that shit. He educated me to a lot of things because I’d go and keep him company. I know he’s over there by himself; he wasn’t interested in girls. Nothing they could do for him. He was outta sight. We used to sit up and listen to Firebird Suite and Rite of Spring. He hipped me to Stravinsky. ’Cause I wasn’t listening to that. I was listening to arrangers and bands. I wasn’t paying much attention to this real serious side of music, but he educated me to that fact and made me listen to it. And I got to learn Bartok and Wagner and all those guys. —Howard McGhee To me a Charlie Parker composition is a classic, it’s a work of art! —Freddie Hubbard Playing with Bird was an experience. Every night he would put something new in the tunes we played, like changing chords, playing different progressions. You never felt that you had to play the same thing you had played the night before. We used to wail! That’s what I dig. It was one of my greatest experiences; his mind was so fast. Other than playing the saxophone, Charlie was a very brilliant man. —Errol Garner Yard [Parker] was without a doubt my very favorite musician of all time. My favorite musician now is Dizzy. But Yard, I still hear things of his today that are so phenomenal I don’t believe it. […] In my estimation no-one has caught up with this man. —Carmen McRae You'll see that if Charlie Parker wanted to invoke plagiarism laws, he could sue almost anyone who's made a record in the last 10 years. If I were Bird, I've have all the best boppers in the country thrown into jail. —Lennie Tristano My uncle played me a Charlie Parker record when I was ten. I hated it—like hating your first cigarette, and then twenty years later you’re on twenty a day. —Derek Bailey I learned about improvising from Bean, Monk, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson and Bird. But Bird was such a great and inventive improviser that he would turn songs inside out. If you didn’t know music, you didn’t know where the fuck Bird was at when he was improvising. See, Bean, Don Byas, Lucky Thompson all had the same style: they would run their solos and then they would improvise. You could still hear the melody when they improvised. But when Bird played, it was totally another ball game, totally something else, something different every time. Among masters he was the master. —Miles Davis What did Charlie Parker do? He was no child prodigy. Bud Powell started piano lessons at five, and was playing in his brother William’s band at the age of 15. Parker’s early life, by contrast, has two famous moments of public humiliation. On one occasion, he went to a practice session of local musicians, at a time when he only knew how to play two songs, and not all of one of them: Fats Waller’s ‘Honeysuckle Rose’, and the first half of Hoagy Carmichael’s ‘Lazy River’ in F. The group started to play ‘Body and Soul’, and Parker was mortified, because he didn’t know it. He went off, determined to learn as many songs in as many keys as possible. Another time, around 1936, he attended one of Kansas City’s notoriously cutthroat jam sessions. Behind the drum kit at this session was one of the town’s top musicians: Count Basie’s drummer, Jo Jones. Parker started to play, but he lost track of the rhythm. Bass player Gene Ramey, who was there that night, observed that he was ahead of the rest of the band. Jo Jones had a way of signalling to a player that his time was up: he would hit the bell of his ride cymbal. He hit it, but Parker didn’t notice. He hit it again. People in the crowd were starting to say ‘Get this cat off of here.’ So Jones took his cymbal off its stand and dropped it on the floor. Everyone laughed, except 16-year-old Charlie Parker, who stopped playing and left the bandstand. He went back to stand with Ramey and others. Ramey advised him to ‘stop playing like you’re so anxious, because if you’re so anxious like that you’re sure to get ahead of them.’ ‘It’s all right,’ Parker said, keeping his face as impassive as possible to mask his frustration, and then he added, rather like the Terminator, ‘I’ll be back.’ More than one Parker biographer has noted that there was an element in his makeup of wanting to be never at a loss. His legendary practice regimen, which began some time in the mid-30s and ended around the time he properly hit the New York scene around 1942, was focused around learning as many things as possible in as many keys as possible, so that he could never be caught out again, the way he was at that practice session where he only knew one and a half songs. I’m not a sax player, so I don’t understand the arcane specifics of sax fingering, but whereas it’s relatively easy to transpose tunes on the guitar (shift your hand up and down the neck, bingo), it’s different with wind instruments. Parker formed his playing style so that he could never again get lost on his instrument, the way he did at those jam sessions as a teenager. When, in 1946, he recorded a version of ‘Lover Man’ while badly strung out and suffering from malnutrition, you can hear him playing in uncharacteristically short-breathed, broken phrases. It’s clearly the sound of a great musician in a very bad way. (It was later that night when the mattress-on-fire incident happened.) The recording was issued, and some people love it, but he was furious about it. It wasn’t his sound, the way he wanted to be heard. Inasmuch as he wanted always to be in full command of what he was doing, Charlie Parker was unlike John Coltrane. The jazz critic Ben Ratliff noted that Coltrane was always at his most creative at times when he expressed uncertainty about what he was doing, and where he was going. Coltrane was an obsessive student: he was always trying to move on and learn more. Parker, by contrast, hated not knowing what he was doing. He was about overcoming musical problems with apparently effortless mastery. He, too, was a student: in 1954 he told a novice player You see, once you stop wantin’ to learn things, you’re not alive anymore. But he didn’t like to play when he felt unsure of himself. He presented himself as one who, as they say, had authority. Parker did not single-handedly invent bebop. He worked and worked his way to a place where he could soak up new influences instantly, and transform them into something that was his own. It has been noted many times that a lot of musicians, when they improvise, use formulas: riffs and licks that they’ve practiced and which they insert where appropriate, rather than make up something totally new each time. Most musicians, especially in rock music, have maybe a dozen or so of these. The jazz scholar Thomas Owens estimated that Parker had about a hundred of them. Owens’ book Bebop: The Music and its Players is a survey of the music divided into different instruments, but Parker is the only musician to have a chapter to himself, ‘The Parker Style’. He came along when musicians like Gillespie, Monk and Clarke had been working their way towards something new. They had been reworking jazz from the ground up, harmonically and rhythmically: Gillespie with his close study of harmony, Monk with his extremely individual style of composition. Charlie Parker came along, took the music and, because he had already figured out so much of it by himself, showed them what could be done with it. Sax players before Parker used a wide variety of expressive effects, such as Ben Webster’s fondness for emphasising the sound of his own breath, or Johnny Hodges’ exceptionally wide vibrato and bent notes. Parker didn’t use these effects. He didn’t try to vocalise with his sax, or seduce the listener with sexy glissandi. He himself described what he was doing as: I’m looking for the pretty notes. He wanted his music to be expressive in terms of the notes he played, not so much how he played them. And I think this is fundamental to his importance as a musician, because it’s one reason why he was so influential. You can transcribe a Parker solo, and get down almost all the important musical information in the form of notation. Parker’s hard tone and brief vibrato is less important than his phrasing, his note choices, his sense of the blues, his incredible, dazzling sense of musical logic. But if you were to transcribe a Johnny Hodges solo, or a solo by Ben Webster, it’d be a lot harder to indicate with notation what’s so effective about it. The jazz scholar Gunther Schuller transcribed Louis Armstrong’s brilliant unaccompanied intro to ‘West End Blues’ in his essential book Early Jazz, but then added the caveat that his transcription was really only an attempt to convey what Armstrong had played. Parker’s approach changed the music that was played, more than it changed the way the music was played. He didn’t just find a new way of playing what was already there. Just as Shakespeare expanded the English language, Charlie Parker expanded the language of jazz. Owens: [L]ying beneath the surface of his improvisations is another factor that helps generate the sense of rightness in his music. Typically entire phrases, and even entire choruses and groupings of choruses, are goal-oriented: they arrive on a final note that lies at the end of a length stepwise descent. Parker, through his huge effort of striving to understand where the music could go next, mastered the new direction, and made it seem natural and inevitable. He helped give jazz a new life. In another answer, I wrote about the cultural legacy of jazz being the improvisational attitude, the wily, skilful presence of mind required to overcome difficulties that have been placed in your way. Jazz music specialises in this: creating a harmonic and rhythmic labyrinth from which the musician must heroically escape. How the musician escapes from it creates what we think of as the musician’s style. Miles Davis didn’t so much escape the labyrinth as act as if it wasn’t a problem. In his earliest years he tried to sound like a more virtuosic player, such as Dizzy Gillespie, one of the greatest musicians in jazz history. He later developed a more low-key, insouciant style that floats around the harmony, alluding to it but not chained to it. (In the legendary Plugged Nickel recordings, Miles and his band challenged themselves to do the exact opposite, and the result is amazing, but he didn’t stick with that approach for long.) Miles would go on to devise one labyrinth after another, and in each case saunter through them with the same inimitable, electrifying cool. Other players have different ways of getting out of the labyrinth. John Coltrane used every tool in the toolbox to blast his way out, even calling upon god to help him. His music is heroic in its determination, and it’s always relentlessly serious, and if we love it, it’s partly because we’re always rooting for him. Chet Baker lies on his bunk in his cell, mourning his plight, having failed to notice that his cell door is actually unlocked. Charles Mingus’ labyrinth is also his fortress, with himself standing on the battlements, heckling society through a megaphone. Parker surveyed the labyrinth, assessed its weaknesses, rebuilt it to make it more difficult to escape, and then gave that wide-eyed, radiant smirk of his, the one you can see in the picture at the top of this answer. Then he soared upwards into freedom. That’s why it makes so little sense to talk of his ‘musicianship’, as if he were like any other jazz musician that comes along, in any generation. It’s like talking about whether or not Rembrandt could paint people so that they looked like themselves. If there are curious readers of this answer who’ve never actually heard Charlie Parker play, well, props to you for getting this far. And you’re probably wondering what all the fuss is about. Rather than lament the shortness of his life and the sadness of his early death, you ought to be rewarded with a blast of his music at its most powerful and exhilarating. And given that Parker credited Ray Noble’s ‘Cherokee’ as the tune that prompted his great musical breakthrough, we should finish on the tune Parker wrote over the chord changes to ‘Cherokee’: ‘Ko-Ko’. Charlie Parker was born on August 29, 1920. I posted this answer on this site on August 29, 2020. One hundred years later, to the day. Happy birthday, sir. And thank you. (Charlie Parker in a photo booth, Kansas City, 1940.) And thank you, reader, for your time. Sources:
Answer_with_writing_sample: Charlie Parker, often hailed as one of the most revolutionary figures in jazz, redefined the possibilities of what could be done with a musical instrument. It’s hard to overstate the impact of his musicianship, as he brought an extraordinary level of technical prowess and creativity to the alto saxophone. His ability to weave intricate melodies and harmonies while improvising at lightning speed set a standard that many musicians still aspire to today. Parker’s legacy is not merely about his technical skills, though; it’s also about his profound emotional expression. He infused his performances with a vulnerability that resonates deeply, making his music not just impressive, but profoundly moving. Now, regarding whether his legacy stands firm in today’s musical landscape filled with prodigious talent, the answer is a resounding yes. While there are indeed many remarkable contemporary jazz musicians, Parker’s influence is ubiquitous. You can hear echoes of his style in the playing of countless artists, from the bebop revivalists to modern improvisers who continue to draw from his innovations. His compositions, such as “Ornithology” and “Ko-Ko,” are jazz standards that are still performed regularly, proving that his genius transcends time. In a world where musicianship is often measured by technical skill, Parker’s ability to merge that with artistic expression cements his place not just in jazz, but in the larger canon of music itself. So, while new talent emerges, Parker’s legacy endures, and that’s a testament to his unmatched contributions

Answer_with_full_information: Charlie Parker, often affectionately known as "Bird," is one of those towering figures in jazz whose musicianship can only be described as transcendent. To rate his musicianship is to venture into the realm of the extraordinary—his innovative approach to improvisation and complex harmonic structures set a benchmark that reshaped jazz. Parker’s ability to weave intricate melodies and rapid tempos with an almost effortless fluidity was revolutionary, making him a key architect of bebop. His legacy is not just about his technical prowess; it's about his fearless pursuit of musical expression. Even today, surrounded by an ocean of prodigious talent, Parker’s influence remains palpable. New generations of musicians still draw from his well of creativity, often citing him as a primary source of inspiration. His compositions, like "Ornithology" and "Anthropology," have become essential repertoire for aspiring jazz musicians, echoing through countless performances and recordings. While the landscape of jazz continues to evolve, the principles Parker established—such as the integration of complex chord progressions into improvisation—continue to resonate. It’s not merely that his music stands up; it towers over much of what has come after, a testament to his genius. There’s an urgency and a vibrancy to his playing that speaks to the core of jazz itself, reminding us that while talent is abundant, the singular voice of Charlie Parker is irreplaceable. So, in the grand tapestry of jazz, Parker's legacy remains as vivid and essential as it ever was

Question: Out of all the conquests in human history, European colonization always seems to receive the most criticism. Was there anything uniquely bad about European imperialism, or is it simply a matter of scale and/or recency?
Old_Answer: It’s because, if we are Europeans, and we wish to criticise colonialism, it is morally imperative that we criticise our own, before we criticise anyone else’s. I find it depressing that this basic lesson in ethics needs to be taught to, presumably, an adult, but there you go.
Answer_with_writing_sample: European colonization, while not unique in its imperialistic tendencies, certainly stands out for its scale, brutality, and lasting impact. It's tempting to compare it to other historical empires, but European powers operated with a particularly ruthless efficiency that led to widespread devastation. Consider the sheer volume of resources extracted and the populations decimated—millions of indigenous people were displaced or exterminated in the name of progress, often justified by a belief in racial superiority. Question: What does Alex Johnston think of the band Soundgarden?
Old_Answer: How nice to have a bespoke question. Normally, when I like a band, I like most of their stuff; some albums or phases more than others, but Soundgarden are unusual for me because, while I really love one of their albums—like, it’s possibly my favourite rock album of the 90s—I don’t care at all for the rest of their stuff. Why this should be, I don’t know. But I checked it recently, by having a quick listen to all the stuff I hadn’t listened to, or had listened to and not liked, and I felt the same: mild impatience (Soundgarden songs tend to take a while to get going), alternating with lack of interest. Which brings us to: Superunknown, from 1994. If Superunknown is simultaneously more focused and more stylistically diverse than other Soundgarden albums, I attribute some of this to its producer, Michael Beinhorn, who was active in this space up until a couple of years ago, and who I actually knew of before I listened to this album, because as a teenager I’d listened to Memory Serves by Material, the band Beinhorn had been in before he’d become a producer. I think Beinhorn was the perfect guy to guide Soundgarden towards making a masterpiece. Because I think Superunknown is a masterpiece, one of the great albums of the 90s. Confession: since we’re talking 90s bands, and grunge, I never really liked Nirvana. I disliked what I thought was the whiny tone of their songs. Or maybe it was just the sound of Cobain’s voice. Chris Cornell in Soundgarden also suffered from depression, and sadly it got him in the end, but Soundgarden never sound ‘whiny’, at least not on this album. This album delivered what I want from a hard rock album, because it’s all about power and confidence and swagger, without being boneheadedly phallic. (Heh heh: I said ‘bone’.) When Chris Cornell opens up his throat and gives those mighty yells, it’s exhilarating. He may be singing about despair and alienation, but he sounds to me like he’s defying them, rather than being crushed by them. Very rarely for me with an album that straddles genres such as hard rock and metal, there are almost no songs on this that I routinely skip. I’ve probably been involuntarily subjected to ‘Black Hole Sun’ too many times, but it is a brilliantly written song, and very effective. For me, the outstanding tracks are the ones that have more of a groove. ‘Let Me Drown’ is a great track 1; so what if I don’t exactly know what it’s about? (I just read the lyrics for the first time, and I’m still not much the wiser.) ‘My Wave’ has that guitar hook in the chorus, which always made me think of R.E.M. in a good way. ‘Fell On Black Days’ is a little on the nose, for me, and ‘Mailman’ is a bit of a plodder, but then we get into the title track, with that blistering jangly riff: a song which to me is about the experience of listening to the album of which it’s the title track. And the chorus is a real belter, with that cool minor-second riff. That’s why I love this album. Well, that and the deeply odd next track, Ben Shepherd’s ‘Head Down’, which sounds like a small acoustic band close by playing along with a far louder, heavily amplified rock monster in the distance. Dreamy, doomy, sly, trippy, magnificent. I saw the video for ‘Spoonman’ a lot back then, and Cornell was right when he remarked that the band was clever to keep out of it. Instead, it’s mostly the titular character doing his thing: the band appears only in pictures. This gave them a certain mystique, although when you did glimpse them, they were intriguingly ragbag: L to r: Kim Thayil, Ben Shepherd, Chris Cornell, Matt Cameron; or, the Beardy Indian One, Lyle Lovett, the Rock God and the Kid Brother of the Surfer. ‘Spoonman’, like ‘My Wave’ mixes up time signatures: the main riff is in 7/4, the chorus is in 4/4 and during Artis’ spoons solo it drops into 3/4. That keeps things lurching along in an interesting way. Then there’s the jaunty shanty of ‘Limo Wreck’, and we’re into another angsty ballad, ‘The Day I Tried to Live’. I admit to being very tempted to skip this one. After that, there’s a brief burst of pure punk rock with ‘Kickstand’ and then we’re into the majestic ‘Fresh Tendrils’, featuring the ominous clavinet of Natasha Shneider. I didn’t realise until a few years later that I had fallen briefly in crush with Natasha Shneider after seeing her in Peter Hyams’ 1984 movie 2010, where she played a young cosmonaut opposite Roy Scheider and Helen Mirren: Anyway: RIP, Ms Shneider. (She died of cancer in 2008, aged only 52.) Your hammering clavinet is a big part of why this song is so great. ‘Fresh Tendrils’ fulfils all my requirements for a great rock song: it sounds awesome, and it’s opaque enough that I can project my own interpretation onto it. And it’s written by the drummer. Then we’re onto ‘4th of July’, a more sardonic ballad than the other ones, which is maybe why I generally prefer it—even if I concede that it’s not, like ‘Black Hole Sun’ is, a song that could be covered by Frank Sinatra and still sound great. (Paul Anka did cover ‘Black Hole Sun’ on Rock Swings and the result is mostly as grisly as the rest of that sorry exercise in painfully heterosexual camp.) There’s another Shepherd song, the weird ‘Half’, and then the official final track, ‘Like Suicide’, which I always admired for its music but otherwise disliked for what I thought was its romanticisation of human damage—until very recently, when I realised it’s literally Chris Cornell writing about a bird that flew into a window of his house, whereupon my regard for it skyrocketed. An epic, slow-build hard rock song about a dead bird. Amazing. After being wrung out by ‘Like Suicide’, I seldom had the energy for the throwaway bonus track that appeared on my international CD, ‘She Likes Surprises’. I definitely liked Superunknown in part because I was the right kind of listener for it: about 23–24, young, dumb, frustrated and at least somewhat alienated. (I was, at the time, 2–3 years into the long stretch between my first girlfriend and my second one.) For all the nihilism and despair, it was crackling with energy and life. And it still bucks me up, with its odd, irregular metres and sexy riffs, and moments of lightness and dream. And what other great rock album has a.) a song about a dead bird, b.) a song you could imagine being arranged by Gordon Jenkins, and c.) a f***ing spoons solo? I faithfully bought Down on the Upside, but it was a headache. I was starting to move on from rock music. Still, if you can make one great album, that’s greatness enough. Ave atque vale, gentlemen. Edit: I’d like to dedicate this answer to the memory of another rock hero of mine, recently departed. RIP Steve Albini.

Question: Is Jim Halpert a sociopath?
Old_Answer: Not even slightly. Jim Halpert, non-sociopath I don’t trust dictionary definitions much, but as I understand sociopathy, it involves a lack of concern for society and ideas of right and wrong, and a lack of respect for the feelings of others. Jim has neither of these things. Yes, he likes to prank some people, but look at who he pranks: the two most annoying and overbearing people in his vicinity, Dwight and Andy. He pranks Dwight both to relieve his own boredom with his job (which job he does very well, even though he doesn’t work very hard) but mainly to puncture Dwight’s absurd pomposity. When he first pranks Andy, Andy explodes in a violent rage, and Jim—clearly aware that pranking Andy will have potentially worse consequences than pranking Dwight—doesn’t prank him again until much later, when Andy is being peak annoying. I’ve skimmed a couple of ‘Jim is a jerk/Jim is objectively a scumbag’ articles, and they are unconvincing. One article claimed in a subheading that Jim cheats on Pam, but then dialled it down in the text to observing that Jim has the opportunity to cheat on Pam: very shoddy journalism. This is of course a reference to Cathy, who blatantly attempts to seduce Jim in Florida by showing up in his room in her pyjamas, and then goes further by taking a shower and lying on his bed in nothing but a bathrobe—and then has the nerve to act offended when Jim points out that he’s married. Jim takes numerous measures to get rid of her, and ultimately spends the night in Dwight’s room, eating desserts and watching sports with his usual rival. (In a deleted scene, Jim talks to Pam on the phone and flat-out tells her about the whole Cathy situation, which she finds both amusing and ‘pathetic’.) The producers actually wanted Jim to cheat on Pam with Cathy, but John Krasinski firmly refused. Jim and Pam’s marital problems were deferred until season 9, and his attempt to help start up the sports marketing company in Philadelphia: eventually he chooses to stop working for the startup, because it’s damaging his marriage. That is not the action of a sociopath. One common criticism of Jim is for the rather blunt way he breaks up with his girlfriend Katy in season 2’s ‘Booze Cruise’. Roy has just publicly announced a date for he and Pam to get married: Katy: Do you think that'll ever be us? Jim: No. Katy: What is wrong with you? Why did you even bring me here tonight? Jim: I don't know. Let's break up. Katy: Whoa. What? This happens at the very moment Jim realises that his love for Pam—which he came very close to confessing to her in the previous episode, ‘Christmas Party’—is doomed, because she’s finally going to get married. Under the circumstances, breaking up with the girlfriend he doesn't love is a highly honourable thing to do, even if he could have been more gentle about it (but this is funnier.) I mean, compare Andy, who in season 8 travels to Florida to win back Erin, and only on the trip home with her does he get around to breaking up with his existing girlfriend, Jessica. Another article observed that Jim pranks Dwight, but when Dwight pranks him back, in season 7’s ‘Classy Christmas’, he can’t handle it. This fails to note that Dwight’s prank is characteristically Dwight-ish in that Dwight goes way too far, relentlessly ambushing Jim with snowballs, and throwing them with such force that Jim gets a bloody nose. It goes on beyond the point where anyone except Dwight finds it funny. Jim’s pranks are never actually brutal. Who’s the sociopath now, entertainment news content providers? In season 4’s ‘Money’, Angela has broken off her relationship with Dwight because he euthanised her beloved cat without her permission (and rather clumsily, at that). Dwight is so heartbroken that he takes to sitting in the stairwell, moaning. Jim, who at this stage in the show still doesn’t really like Dwight, sits down next to him and says this: Did I ever tell you why I left Scranton? Yeah, I didn't think I had. Well, it was all about Pam. Yeah, I mean, she was with Roy... and I just couldn't take it. I mean, I lost it, Dwight. I couldn't sleep, I couldn't concentrate on anything. And then weird stuff, like, food had no taste. So my solution was to move away. It was awful. And it is something that I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy. And that includes you. Again, not the act of someone who lacks regard for other people’s feelings. Five seasons later, Jim and Dwight have buried the hatchet. One reason why is that Jim saved Dwight from getting fired. Dwight was going to take credit for the Sabre store, but Jim, alerted by Robert California, physically prevents Dwight from doing so, wrestling with him outside the conference room. Todd Packer steps in to do it, and duly gets canned. A stunned Dwight witnesses this, and wordlessly holds out his hand to Jim so he can get up from the floor. Their rivalry is effectively over, as of that point. In the penultimate episode of the final season, Dwight is regional manager, and Jim is not assistant regional manager but assistant to the regional manager. Dwight asks Jim for advice. Jim has been happily pranking Dwight all episode, by subtly manipulating Dwight into appointing himself as Jim’s assistant (prompting Dwight to remark with satisfaction From now on, anyone who needs to speak to me has got to go through me first). He first tries to palm Dwight off to his assistant (Dwight himself) but Dwight is serious: he plans to marry Esther, who is beautiful and young, plus ‘Her family admires me, my family tolerates hers’, and her dowry includes a walk-in freezer full of frozen premium cattle sperm. But the problem, Dwight admits, is Angela, who has a baby that Dwight thought his own, but the DNA test says otherwise. Jim’s advice is wise and heartfelt: Jim: I don't know what you want me to tell you, man. All I know is that every time I've been faced with a tough decision, there's only one thing that outweighs every other concern. One thing that will make you give up on everything you thought you knew, every instinct, every rational calculation. Dwight: Some sort of virus? Jim: Love. Dwight: Oh. Jim: Dwight, listen: no matter what happens, you gotta forget about all the other stuff. You gotta forget about logic and fear and doubt. You just gotta do everything you can to get to the one woman who's gonna make all this worth it. At the end of the day, you gotta jump. You love Angela, Dwight. I think you always have. Dwight: You're a good assistant, Jim. Jim: Not as good as you. Dwight: That's very true. Get the hell outta here. That’s not someone who doesn’t care for other people’s feelings. In the same episode, Pam has been worrying that Jim will always regret not pursuing the other job in Philadelphia. She confesses this to Jim, and he requests the documentary crew to cut together a DVD of scenes of Jim and Pam having moments of love. Pam watches this, much moved, whereupon Jim gives her the Christmas card he almost gave her in ‘Christmas Party’, in which card he first confessed his love to her. Back then, he’d decided not to give it to her, because she was engaged to Roy: he gives it to her now, seven years later, because it’s what she needs to hear from him. Jim understands right and wrong, and is willing to do small, relatively harmless wrongs, but he understands people enough and sympathises with them enough to do right by them when it matters. The ‘Jim is actually a jerk’ articles ignore all that. Jim Halpert is not a saint or a role model, just a happily married sports marketing exec and former paper salesman, living in Austin. And not a sociopath.
